In FY 2025–26, the Rakshak pilot at 
the Coke Oven unit of Dolvi Works was successfully completed and is now being scaled across the full Dolvi Steel facility, with planned coverage extending to approximately 14,000 personnel, making it one of the most extensive connected worker deployments in the Indian steel industry. In parallel, a pilot deployment was initiated at SMS#2 of Vijayanagar Steel, setting the stage for further Group-wide rollout. The platform enhances ground-level visibility, reduces response times to safety alerts and provides management with actionable data to drive proactive interventions.
Bow-Tie Barrier Management
Process safety management at complex industrial facilities requires a structured methodology for understanding, monitoring and strengthening the barriers that prevent major accidents. We deployed the Bow-Tie Barrier Management methodology across Vijayanagar, Dolvi, BPSL and Salem, supported by expert-led training programmes. The Bow-Tie model enables the systematic identification of top process safety events, the mapping of preventive and mitigative controls (barriers), and the assessment of barrier effectiveness.
This approach moves safety management 
beyond incident response towards proactive risk control, ensuring that critical barriers are maintained, tested, and continuously improved. By embedding Bow-Tie analysis into site safety reviews, we have significantly enhanced our ability to prevent major process safety incidents and protect both people and assets.
PQA and CARES Audits for 
Contractors
Contractors represent a substantial 
proportion of our operational workforce and their safety performance is integral to our Company’s overall safety record. In FY 2025-26, Pre-Qualification Audits (PQA) and CARES (Contractor Assessment and Rating for Excellence in Safety) audits were completed for over 3,500+ contractors.These audits evaluate contractors against rigorous criteria including safety management systems, training standards, equipment compliance, incident history and supervisory capability. The outcomes drive contractor selection, performance improvement plans and where necessary, deselection of non-compliant vendors. This systematic approach to contractor safety governance ensures that our safety standards are embedded throughout our extended value chain.
Progressive Consequence 
Management (PCM) framework
Consistent enforcement of safety rules 
is essential to sustaining a culture of accountability. In FY 2025-26, a Progressive Consequence Management (PCM) framework was standardised across all ISPs and Coated units. The PCM framework establishes a structured, transparent and graduated approach to addressing safety violations from coaching and counselling for minor infractions to stronger measures for repeat or severe violations.
By ensuring that consequences are 
proportionate, predictable and fairly applied, the PCM framework reinforces the message that safety rules are non-negotiable while also ensuring that interventions are constructive and oriented towards behaviour change rather than punitive. This standardisation eliminates inconsistency across sites and strengthens the integrity of the safety management system.05 /  SUSTAINABILITY  /  SOCIAL
Safety Reward and Recognition 
Guidelines
Positive reinforcement is as important as 
consequence management in shaping safety behaviour. In FY 2025–26, Group-wide Safety Reward and Recognition Guidelines were established to institutionalise a consistent framework for recognising exemplary safety contributions across all sites. These guidelines ensure that individuals and teams who demonstrate outstanding safety leadership, innovation, or performance are recognised in a timely, meaningful and visible manner-reinforcing the behaviours the organisation seeks to promote and creating role models for the broader workforce.
National Safety Week 2026 and 
Road Safety Week
Our commitment to safety culture is 
reflected in how we celebrate and engage our workforce on safety themes throughout the year. In FY 2025–26, National Safety Week 2026 was observed across all sites with a rich programme of quizzes, awareness video screenings, safety skits, VR experience sessions and reward-based activities, all aligned to the theme ‘Safety and Well-Being are the Drivers for Crucial Change’. Road Safety Week was similarly observed with targeted campaigns reinforcing road safety awareness for employees and contractors. These events serve not only to commemorate safety milestones but also to sustain year-round momentum and create shared experiences that strengthen collective safety ownership.Competent Workforce
A Zero Harm workplace can only be achieved when every member of the workforce from senior engineers to entry-level contractors, possesses the technical knowledge, practical skills and behavioural competencies to perform their work safely. Our workforce development strategy is therefore grounded in a continuous cycle of assessment, targeted training and practical reinforcement, ensuring that competence is built, verified and sustained over time. In FY 2025–26, we significantly expanded the scale and sophistication of our workforce development interventions.
Skill and competency  
assessments at scale
In FY 2025–26, over 78,000 workmen underwent structured skill and competency assessments, a transformational increase from the 2,012 assessed in FY 2024–25, reflecting our Company’s decisive commitment to building a comprehensively assessed and verifiably competent workforce. These assessments cover critical safety domains including Lockout Tagout, Work at Height, Scaffolding, Machine Guarding, Conveyor Safety, Electrical Safety, Road Safety, Contractor Safety Management, Confined Space and Crane Safety evaluating both technical knowledge and practical application skills.
The outcomes of these assessments 
directly inform personalised training interventions, ensuring that skill gaps are addressed in a targeted and resource-efficient manner and that each worker receives the specific development they need to perform their role safely.
Subject Matter Expert (SME) 
Programme
Deep technical expertise is essential 
to the credibility and effectiveness of our safety management system. In FY 2025-26, the Subject Matter Expert (SME) programme launched in July 2024 certified over 3,000 employees across 15 Group Health and Safety Standards, encompassing critical areas including Lockout Tagout, Work at Height, Scaffolding, Machine Guarding and Conveyor Safety, among others.
The programme also certified over 
300 ‘Train the Trainer’ (ToT) facilitators, building an internal training infrastructure capable of sustaining and scaling safety competency development without dependence on external resources. This creates a self-reinforcing ecosystem of expertise where certified SMEs and trainers continuously build the capability of their peers and the broader workforce.
Process Safety Competency 
Development Programme
Process safety, the discipline of 
preventing catastrophic incidents arising from the unintended release of energy or hazardous materials, requires a specialised and advanced level of technical competency. In FY 2025-26, we launched a Process Safety Competency Development Programme in strategic partnership with dss+ (formerly DuPont Sustainable Solutions), a globally recognised leader in process safety consulting and training.
This programme focuses on building 
deep technical capability in process hazard analysis, layer of protection analysis, management of change and process safety auditing, equipping O&M and HSE professionals with the skills to identify and manage process safety risks at our complex, high-hazard manufacturing facilities.
TapRooT® Advanced RCA Team 
Leader Training
The quality of incident investigation is one of the most significant determinants of an organisation’s ability to prevent recurrence. Superficial investigations that identify proximate causes without addressing underlying systemic factors create a false sense of closure and leave root causes intact. In FY 2025–26, we equipped 119 O&M and HSE professionals with

Safety Experience Centres
Traditional classroom-based safety training is often insufficient to prepare workers for the hazards they will encounter in real-world industrial environments. We have addressed this limitation by investing in state-of-the-art Safety Experience Centres at Vijayanagar, Dolvi, BPSL and Salem Works — all of which are now fully operational.
These centres offer immersive, scenario-
based training environments that recreate actual workplace hazards, including confined space emergencies, working at height scenarios, electrical safety simulations, and struck-by hazards in a safe, controlled setting. By experiencing hazards in a realistic environment before encountering them on the job, workers develop sharper hazard recognition skills, stronger muscle memory for safe behaviours and a more profound appreciation of the consequences of unsafe actions. A new Safety Experience Centre is under development at Salem to further expand this capability.
Digital Visual Platform (DVP)
We have deployed the Digital Visual Platform (DVP) across our operations in FY 2025–26, enabling real-time applications for PPE violation detection, unauthorised parking, crowd detection and other safety compliance monitoring with AI-generated real-time alerts and automated reports. This technology-enabled approach to safety monitoring provides management with continuous, objective feedback on compliance levels across large, complex operational areas.
Continuous cultural engagement
Building and sustaining a safety culture requires constant, consistent engagement across the workforce, not just during formal training events or safety week celebrations. We maintain year-round workforce engagement through monthly safety campaigns, toolbox talks, incident review sessions, safety skits and peer-to-peer safety conversations.
Continuous engagement has deepened 
the personal connection of every member of the workforce to safety culture, reinforcing the principle that safety is not a departmental responsibility but a shared commitment at every level of our Company.
Digitalisation  
and innovation 
Technology is a powerful force multiplier for safety management, enabling faster decision-making, broader reach, deeper analytics and more consistent compliance monitoring than is possible through manual processes alone. We have made digitalisation and innovation a defining pillar of our safety strategy, deploying a suite of cutting-edge tools and platforms that are transforming how safety is managed, monitored and learned across our operations.
Abhigyan – industry-first 
conversational ai safety tool
In FY 2025–26, we achieved a landmark 
in industrial safety technology with the launch of ‘Abhigyan’ at Dolvi Steel, an industry-first conversational AI tool that provides employees and contract workers with real-time, multilingual access to our integrated safety standards. Abhigyan leverages advanced natural language processing to allow workers to query safety procedures, permit requirements, emergency protocols and regulatory standards in their preferred language, through a conversational interface that requires no technical expertise to use.
This innovation addresses one of the most 
persistent challenges in industrial safety, ensuring that all workers, including those with limited literacy or digital skills, have immediate access to the information they need to perform their work safely. Abhigyan democratises safety knowledge and eliminates language and literacy barriers as obstacles to safe behaviour.
Electronic Permit to Work (E-PTW)
The Permit to Work (PTW) system is one of the most critical controls for managing high-risk work activities such as confined space entry, hot work, work at height and electrical isolation. Historically, paper-based PTW systems have been prone to errors, delays, inconsistency and loss of documentation, creating significant compliance risks.
In FY 2025-26, we implemented Electronic 
Permit to Work (E-PTW) systems across key sites, digitising the entire permit lifecycle from application and approval to issuance, extension and closure. E-PTW ensures that all permits are complete, consistent and traceable; that approvals involve the right personnel; and that real-time data on active high-risk work is available to safety managers at all times. The system also enables trend analysis on permit compliance, providing early warning of deteriorating standards before incidents occur.
Digital Visual Platform (DVP) – AI-
powered compliance monitoring
We deployed the Digital Visual Platform 
(DVP) across our operations in FY 2025-26, using artificial intelligence and computer vision to provide real-time monitoring of safety compliance across operational areas. DVP applications include automated detection of PPE non-compliance (helmets, vests, gloves, footwear), unauthorised access to restricted areas, unsafe parking and crowd density monitoring in high-risk zones.
The platform generates real-time alerts 
to supervisors, enabling immediate intervention before unsafe conditions escalate into incidents. Automated reports provide management with objective, site-wide data on compliance trends, enabling targeted interventions and resource allocation. By removing the dependence on manual observation for compliance monitoring, DVP significantly extends the reach and consistency of safety oversight across large, complex facilities.
Virtual Reality (VR) training 
modules
Virtual Reality (VR) technology enables 
immersive, experiential safety training that is fundamentally more engaging and effective than conventional classroom instruction. In FY 2025–26, we deployed VR-based training modules covering critical hazard scenarios including Conveyor Safety, Lancing Safety and a range of other high-risk activities with over 11,000 contractor workers trained through 22 Virtual Reality modules during the year.
VR training places workers in a 
photorealistic simulation of their actual work environment, exposing them to hazard scenarios and emergency situations that would be too dangerous to recreate in reality. Research consistently demonstrates that VR training produces superior knowledge retention, hazard recognition and decision-making under pressure compared to traditional training methods. By integrating VR into its safety training architecture, we are delivering training that not only educates but truly prepares our workforce for the hazards they face.
Sustainability-linked 
remuneration
At JSW Steel, Environment, Social and 
Governance (ESG) criteria are embedded in leadership performance evaluations and serve as a critical pillar of executive accountability. ESG forms a mandatory Key Result Area (KRA) for the assessment of our top leadership, including Executive Directors, where it carries a significant weightage of 15% to 20% in their individual KRAs linked to the annual variable payout. This direct alignment between ESG outcomes and executive remuneration reflects our Company’s commitment to responsible value creation and highlights the strategic importance placed on safety, sustainability, equity and governance.
The evaluation of senior leadership includes 
structured targets across key ESG themes. These outcomes influence compensation decisions and reinforce leadership responsibility for advancing our Company’s sustainability agenda.
Translating ESG themes into 
measurable performance outcomes

Equity Action

These ESG-linked measures have been

in FY 2025-26.Acknowledging the nexus between  
social sustainability and value creation
While social sustainability is undeniably a critical fiduciary responsibility for our business, we see it as much more than that. At JSW Steel, we view social sustainability as a powerful yet often under-recognised lever for long-term value creation. While the role of such initiatives in advancing the socio-economic upliftment of marginalised and underserved communities by, among other things, alleviating hunger, improving literacy, and enhancing health and sanitation is widely acknowledged, we believe their broader strategic business value is often overlooked. Besides delivering meaningful outcomes for stakeholders, social sustainability efforts can also beget a plethora of benefits for businesses, including unlocking new markets, shoring up key stakeholder relationships, bolstering reputational capital, improving employee engagement and retention, and catalysing innovation. In coherence with this understanding, this year, we intensified our efforts endeavouring to further ingrain social sustainability into the very core of our Company's value creation strategy and purpose. This move reflects our belief that a company's success remains deeply intertwined with the well-being of its communities and that a commitment to social impact is essential for sustainable, long-term growth.
SAMMS approach
We recognise that translating our social sustainability vision into tangible action requires adopting a structured approach that enables us to design and implement high-impact interventions, monitor and evaluate their outcomes, and forge trust-based partnerships with the communities we serve. Therefore, we adopt the Strategic, Aligned, Multi-Stakeholders, Measurable, Sustainable (SAMMS) approach. This approach, which now underpins the full portfolio of our social sustainability initiatives, ensures that our social sustainability initiatives directly align with our broader organisational objectives, foster community engagement, and deliver measurable results. The adoption of this robust methodology has enabled us to deliver consistent and lasting impact in the communities where we operate.

Lives touchedHealth and Nutrition
Reliable healthcare and adequate nutrition are not only fundamental 
human rights but also essential development priorities under the UN SDGs that India must strive to advance as it progresses along its growth trajectory. We remain deeply committed to driving progress on these fronts. Therefore, we have set a mission to contribute to a healthier and better-nourished nation through initiatives that revolve around three core pillars: community interventions, institution-building, and comprehensive healthcare programmes tailored to local needs.
Bolstering emergency 
response capabilities for underserved communities through free ambulance services
Ambulances serve as the arteries of any 
robust public healthcare system. They not only enable rapid emergency response and timely medical intervention but also play a pivotal role in bridging the accessibility gap by connecting remote communities to essential healthcare services. That said, several regions continue to face a severe shortage of ambulances, which further exacerbates several challenges such as delayed medical attention and preventable fatalities. Thus, in an effort to tackle this challenge, we operate round-the-clock free ambulance services across seven Indian states. Over the years, this service has provided critical assistance to thousands of individuals encountering life-threatening situations, including road accidents and other incidents causing severe physical trauma.Bridging healthcare gaps 
in geographically isolated communities through mobile health units
It is an unfortunate reality that 
geographically isolated communities often lack access to quality healthcare, which is typically concentrated in or around major urban centres and population hubs. This lack of accessible and reliable healthcare results in a persistent healthcare gap, where these communities are unable to seek care and treatment when they need it most. To help address this challenge, which undermines the well-being of these populations and stymies their productivity and, by extension, upward mobility, we operate a fleet of Mobile Health Units (MHUs). These vehicles, equipped with essential diagnostic tools, a wide range of generic and essential medications, and staffed by experienced medical professionals, aim to expand healthcare access by bringing quality medical services to underserved and geographically isolated communities. Over the years, our MHUs have served thousands of individuals in need, offering timely care, improving health outcomes among highly vulnerable populations, and reinforcing our mission of ensuring equitable access to healthcare for all Indians.

Education
Ensuring that all citizens have access to high-quality, accessible 
education is essential for fostering upward social mobility, propelling economic growth, and cultivating a well-informed citizenry. While India is widely extolled as a breeding ground for groundbreaking thinkers and some of the brightest minds globally, significant barriers to quality education persist for many sections of the population. We remain committed to bridging these accessibility gaps by implementing targeted educational initiatives that improve learning outcomes and teaching infrastructure in underserved regions.
Laying the building blocks 
for lifelong learning: Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE)
Ample empirical evidence suggests that 
the period from birth to eight years of age is pivotal for a child’s cognitive, emotional, and social development. Marked by rapid brain growth, this stage offers a critical window of opportunity to lay a strong academic foundation, promote healthy socialisation, and foster overall well-being. Unfortunately, children from marginalised and underserved communities often fail to receive the academic and developmental exposure they need during this formative phase due to a combination of factors, including limited access to early childhood education, inadequate infrastructure, a shortage of trained educators, and socio-economic challenges within their households.14,990 Students benefittedHumraahi: Advancing the 
health and well-being of 
India’s trucking community
The trucking community plays an 
instrumental role in facilitating the transport of inputs, finished products, and essential supplies within the steel sector and, more broadly, across all basic materials industries. Without a reliable trucking network, the manufacturing sector as we know it risks coming to a standstill. Despite the instrumental role truckers play in supporting economic growth and ensuring the continuity of the manufacturing sector's operations, they remain heavily underserved by public health systems. This lack of access to quality healthcare, coupled with challenging working conditions characterised by long hours, limited access to healthy food, and chronic sleep deprivation, renders truckers disproportionately vulnerable to a wide range of communicable and non-communicable diseases, including obesity, hypertension, diabetes, sleep apnea, cardiovascular diseases, and respiratory problems. Therefore, to help address these health risks, we launched Humraahi – Holistic Wellness for Truck Drivers in Vijayanagar, Karnataka. 
Since its inception in 2010, Humraahi 
has benefited thousands of truckers by providing vital healthcare services, including general health check-ups, screenings for diabetes and hypertension, vision care, road safety awareness sessions, de-addiction support, and HIV/AIDS prevention initiatives. Through these measures, Humraahi has not only improved the health outcomes of truck drivers but also contributed to safer roads, reduced absenteeism, and enhanced the overall well-being of our trucking community.JSW Centre on Climate 
Change and Health: Addressing climate change as a threat multiplier for public health
It is widely recognised in both academic 
and public health circles that climate change acts as a threat multiplier; and as such, it has the potential to aggravate a multitude of health risks, ranging from heat-related illnesses and respiratory conditions to vector-borne diseases and malnutrition. 
Consequently, effective climate change 
adaptation strategies must develop a nuanced understanding of how climate change exacerbates existing health challenges and institute proactive measures to mitigate these threats; as a failure to do so risks overwhelming public health systems, eroding their resilience, and disproportionately affecting vulnerable and marginalised groups such as the elderly, children, low-income communities, and those with pre-existing health conditions. In doing so, it spotlights our commitment to strengthening the adaptive capacity of the communities we serve against the multifaceted threats posed by climate change, particularly those related to health, and to fostering the development of evidence-based public health systems capable of maintaining resilience in the face of a warming planet.

Water, Environment and Sanitation
Water, environment, and sanitation represent cross-cutting issues 
at the very heart of community well-being. Water security, a healthy environment, and robust sanitation are not only critical for sustaining human health and preventing communicable diseases but are also fundamental to economic growth, social equity, and environmental resilience. Therefore, we strive to implement targeted interventions that augment access to potable water, promote the responsible stewardship of sensitive ecosystems, and encourage the uptake of sound sanitation practices. Through such efforts, we aim to empower the communities we serve to lead healthier lives and foster the sustainable use and management of resources and ecosystem services to safeguard their availability for future generations.
Improving climate 
resilience through water interventions
Climate change poses multifaceted 
physical risks, including but not limited to an increased frequency of extreme weather events and rising sea levels. Certain climate change-induced physical risks, such as the heightened occurrence and intensity of floods and droughts, can erode water security and thereby constrain communities' access to the freshwater resources essential for domestic use, agriculture, and sanitation, thereby undermining their socio-economic well-being.
Recognising such threats, we have 
intensified our efforts aimed at equipping vulnerable communities with the tools, resources, and expertise needed to effectively adapt to shifting freshwater availability patterns effectuated by climate change. Over the past year, we implemented a range of initiatives focused on strengthening watershed management and storage infrastructure, establishing NbS, and constructing solar-powered bore wells. These solutions were strategically aligned with the goals of the Jal Jeevan Mission, a state-sponsored programme by the Government of India aiming to 7.86 lakh m3 Increase in ground 
water recharge capacity
provide safe and adequate drinking water to every rural household, and they are playing a vital role in enhancing water security and building long-term resilience among populations disproportionately susceptible to climate change-associated water impacts.
Transforming sanitation 
infrastructure for underserved populations: WaSH Programme
Sanitation and health are closely 
interconnected, with strong sanitation practices leading to better health outcomes. With this understanding, we launched the WaSH programme—an integrated water, sanitation, and hygiene initiative designed to improve access to functional toilets, safe drinking water, and menstrual hygiene for underserved communities. Since its inception, the WaSH programme has expanded its reach to 135 villages and positively impacted nearly 12,600 households through the provision of targeted subsidies. Since the high upfront costs entailed by the construction of sanitation facilities, such as toilets and related infrastructure, remain a significant obstacle hindering their proliferation in rural areas, these subsidies are playing a vital role in making sanitation solutions more accessible, affordable, and sustainable for low-income communities. 
The WaSH programme's interventions 
are not limited to rural regions. As part of this initiative, we have also developed a series of public hygiene solutions in urban settings, including community wash centers, mobile toilet units, and handwashing stations, in cities across India. We envisage these solutions as critical infrastructure that address the immediate sanitation needs of densely populated urban areas while simultaneously laying the groundwork for a healthier and more resilient population.
Reconnecting communities 
with nature through tree plantation
It is well-established that human alienation 
from nature can exacerbate environmental degradation. In contrast, when individuals cultivate a deeper connection with the natural world, they often become more responsible stewards, learn to live in symbiosis with nature, and treat their environment with greater respect, care, and sensitivity. Acknowledging this relationship, we strive to help communities across the nation foster closer ties with nature and, in doing so, promote more eco-conscious behaviours. One of our key efforts involves organising large-scale tree plantation drives, where community members are invited to plant saplings carefully selected to align with local soil and climatic conditions. Through their participation in such initiatives, local communities not only develop closer ties with nature but also tangibly contribute to healthier and more resilient ecosystems. We have already conducted such drives near our ISP in Vijayanagar, at the Miyawaki forests in Vasind, and in the Mahavanam project in Salem. Over the coming years, we plan to expand these initiatives and organise similar drives in additional locations across the country.1,56,524 Tree saplings planted135 Villages impacted

Waste Management
India, by dint of its large population and extensive manufacturing

Art, culture and heritage
India is a nation steeped in a rich history of eclectic art forms, vibrant cultural 
traditions, and a heritage that spans thousands of years. Art, culture, and heritage are not only vital sources of national pride but also form a critical component of national identity and social cohesion. While they serve as a bridge connecting past and present, foster community resilience, and offer opportunities for employment and economic growth, they face the risk of erosion and gradual extinction in the absence of sustained preservation efforts and policies that recognise their intrinsic, cultural, and economic value. Hence, we have launched several initiatives that preserve traditional arts and crafts, revive those that have lost prominence, and empower artisans skilled in these time-honoured practices, thereby ensuring future generations have the opportunity to witness and bask in the pleasure of these cultural treasures for years to come.
Where heritage inspires tomorrow
Set against the timeless backdrop of Hampi, home to the architectural grandeur and cultural legacy of the 
Vijayanagara Empire, JSW Foundation has created Hampi Art Labs, its flagship initiative dedicated to advancing art, culture and heritage. Located near JSW Steel’s Vijayanagar operations and launched in February 2024, the centre reflects over three decades of the Foundation’s commitment to preserving and promoting India’s cultural landscape. Founded by Sangita Jindal and Tarini Jindal Handa, Hampi Art Labs has been envisioned as an interdisciplinary institution where artists and creative practitioners can immerse themselves in a setting shaped by centuries of artistic excellence and cultural exchange.
Spread across a nine-acre campus near the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Hampi, the centre brings together 
exhibition galleries, artist studios, landscaped gardens, residential facilities and collaborative spaces designed to nurture creativity. Through one- to three-month residency programmes, artists across disciplines are provided with world-class infrastructure, production capabilities and an inspiring environment to deepen their practice. Surrounded by the Tungabhadra River, dramatic boulder-strewn landscapes and the enduring spirit of one of India’s greatest civilisations, Hampi Art Labs stands as a living platform where heritage, nature and contemporary creativity converge to shape new cultural narratives.A new chapter for a timeless institution
As part of its commitment to preserving India’s cultural and architectural heritage, JSW Foundation has partnered with the David Sassoon Library and Reading Room through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to support the conservation and restoration of one of Mumbai’s most iconic institutions. Located in the historic Kala Ghoda precinct, the Grade I heritage structure, established in 1870, is among the city’s oldest surviving libraries and a landmark of enduring intellectual and cultural significance. Through technical and financial support, JSW Foundation is contributing to the revival of this historic institution, ensuring that its legacy continues to inspire future generations.
The restoration initiative brings together a coalition of organisations, including Hermès, the Kala Ghoda Association, the Consulate 
General of Israel in Mumbai and other stakeholders to collectively safeguard this architectural treasure. Led by renowned conservation architect Abha Narain Lambah, the restoration aims to revive the library’s original character, preserving its distinctive buff-coloured trachyte and limestone architecture while enhancing its longevity. Through this initiative, JSW Foundation is helping transform heritage conservation into a shared endeavour, protecting not only a building, but a living repository of knowledge, memory and civic identity.Hampi Art Labs

 HUMAN RIGHTSValues driven by people
We view the protection of 
human rights not merely as a compliance requirement but as a core expression of our values and commitment to promoting diversity, equity and inclusion and uplifting the communities in  
which we operate.05 /  SUSTAINABILITY  /  HUMAN RIGHTS
In line with our commitment to operationalising the triple bottom line framework, which 
treats people, planet, and profit as equally vital measures of business success, we strive to treat every individual connected to our operations, be it employees, business partners, contract workers, or surrounding communities with dignity, respect, and fairness. 
To translate this belief into meaningful action, we have built a robust human rights 
governance structure anchored in four key pillars: building awareness across the value chain, identifying and evaluating potential risks, designing targeted mitigation strategies, and ensuring continuous oversight through regular progress reviews. This structured approach enables us to move beyond intent and embed human rights considerations into the fabric of our day-to-day decision-making across all operational levels.
Approach to human rights management
Our approach to human rights management is grounded in the conviction that respecting and protecting human rights is an active, ongoing responsibility—not merely a passive obligation satisfied by regulatory compliance alone. To instil this conviction at the heart of our operational ethos, we have adopted a comprehensive Policy on Protecting Human Rights, supported by an internal Technical Standard that provides operational guidance on identifying material human rights issues, assigning accountability, and implementing effective management systems and procedures across our operations.
Our human rights framework ensures full compliance with all applicable national and 
international laws, regulations, and standards, including the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the core conventions of the International Labor Organization, and the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. We also transparently disclose our human rights performance through the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) standards, against the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs), and under Principle 5 of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct (NGRBC) as part of our Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR).
Our commitment to human rights is further reinforced by three interrelated policies that 
govern how we engage with our workforce, our communities, and our broader value chain: the Policy on Labour Practices and Employment Rights, the Policy on Enhancing Equality, 
Diversity and Inclusivity, and the Policy on Business Conduct. In tandem with our Policy on Protecting Human Rights, these policies form a cohesive governance architecture that embeds respect for human rights into the way we operate, make decisions, and conduct business at every level of our organisation.Capitals interlinkages

As of FY 2025–26, we have achieved 100% HRDD coverage across all our Integrated Steel 
Plants (ISPs) and mines. Through comprehensive HRDD risk assessments, we proactively identify, assess, and address actual and potential human rights impacts across both our operations and value chain, ensuring that every facility we operate upholds the highest standards of ethical conduct, dignity, and fairness.
Beyond mitigating risks, our HRDD process serves a broader strategic purpose. It allows 
us to cultivate deeper understanding of the communities in which we operate, strengthen engagement with rights holders, and ensure that our presence creates lasting social value. By systematically evaluating our human rights performance and translating insights into targeted management actions, we move beyond compliance to uphold human rights across operations, while contributing to community well-being and sustainable development.
We extend our HRDD framework to all new business relationships, including mergers, 
acquisitions, and joint ventures, integrating human rights considerations into investment and business decisions from the earliest stages of engagement.
Human rights risk assessments, which form the cornerstone of our HRDD process, 
follow the structured five-step methodology detailed below.Identified rights holders
Our commitment to respecting and upholding human rights extends to all individuals who our operations and activities may affect across the value chain. Thus, our HRDD process covers a broad range of key rights holders: employees, contract workers (including migrant workers), local communities and societies (with particular attention to women, children, and Indigenous Peoples), suppliers, and customers.
Actions taken to advance human 
rights across operations in FY 2025-26
As of FY 2025–26, all our ISPs (Vijayanagar, 
Dolvi, Salem, and Raigarh) and mining operations across Karnataka and Odisha have been assessed under our Human Rights Due Diligence (HRDD) process, achieving full coverage of our operational and mining footprint. During the year, we also initiated a Human Rights Risk Assessment for JSW Utkal Steel Limited, our under-construction greenfield ISP at Paradeep, Odisha. This reflects our commitment to embedding human rights considerations into project planning from the earliest stages of development and consistently applying our HRDD framework across our expanding portfolio.
We leverage the insights gained through 
the HRDD process to formulate site-specific human rights management plans. These plans delve into the intricacies of each site's unique social context, meticulously outline measures for risk mitigation, delineate clear roles and responsibilities, assign appropriate authorities, and set specific targets to ensure the protection and promotion of human rights within our operational sphere.
This year, we also conducted targeted 
human rights training and awareness programmes for employees, business partners, and security personnel across our facilities. These initiatives sought to strengthen understanding of human rights principles, clarify roles and responsibilities, and reinforce standards of conduct, thereby fostering a culture of respect, accountability, and responsible business practices throughout our operations.
Embedding Rights-Based 
Thinking into Greenfield Development: Human 
Rights Due Diligence at JSW Utkal Steel Limited, Paradeep
Industrial expansion is not solely 
an engineering endeavour; it is a social undertaking in equal measure. Decisions made during the planning, construction, and operation of a new facility have far-reaching implications for the rights, livelihoods, and well-being of workers, neighbouring communities, and other rights holders, while also shaping local economies and long-term development outcomes.
In FY 2025-26, we initiated the HRDD 
process at JSW Utkal Steel Limited, our under-construction greenfield Integrated Steel Plant in Jagatsinghpur district, Odisha, by conducting a Human Rights Risk Assessment (HRRA) through an independent external agency. The assessment examined the potential impacts of pre-construction and construction activities on workers, neighbouring communities, and other affected stakeholders, benchmarked project practices against internationally recognised frameworks—including the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs), the ResponsibleSteel™ Standard, and the International Labour Organization (ILO) Core Principles—and identified opportunities to further strengthen our human rights management framework.
The assessment adopted a robust and 
participatory methodology, combining desktop research, site inspections, and extensive stakeholder engagement. Consultations were undertaken with project management, contractors, workers, local administrative authorities, tribal welfare associations, civil society organisations, and communities across PARADEEP
villages within the project's area of influence. These engagements explored a broad range of issues, including land acquisition, livelihoods, environmental impacts, occupational health and safety, worker welfare, grievance mechanisms, and access to effective remedy.
Following the completion of fieldwork, all 
identified issues were evaluated using a structured risk matrix that considered their scope, scale, remediability, and likelihood. The findings were consolidated into a comprehensive risk register, supported by prioritised mitigation actions, clearly defined ownership, and implementation timelines. While the assessment identified opportunities for improvement, appropriate corrective actions have since been initiated and integrated into the project's ongoing human rights management framework, reinforcing our commitment to responsible project development from inception through operation.05 /  SUSTAINABILITY  /  HUMAN RIGHTS

 SUPPLY CHAIN  
SUSTAINABILITY Impact across value chain
We consider fostering the 
adoption of more sustainable practices across our supply chain as a powerful lever for not only managing Scope 3 emissions more effectively but also generating measurable environmental and social impact across the value chain.05 /  SUSTAINABILITY  /  SUPPLY CHAIN SUSTAINABILITY
In recent years, forging sustainable 
supply chains has emerged as a strategic imperative for businesses operating in the manufacturing sector, where horizontally integrated production systems rely on complex global procurement and distribution networks. Due to such interdependencies, sustainability risks and opportunities often spill over across multiple businesses’ value chains, making supply chain transformation paramount for achieving enterprise-level ESG objectives.
In the global steel sector’s context, the 
heterogeneity of inputs and geographically dispersed supplier bases further exacerbate this challenge by diminishing transparency. At JSW Steel, however, we believe this challenge presents an equally compelling opportunity to stimulate collaboration and collective action.In pursuit of this vision, we published a Supplier Code of Conduct (SCoC) in 2021. This document delineates a set of minimum environmental, social, and governance standards that suppliers must satisfy to enter into, or continue doing business with, our Company. Regardless, we fully acknowledged that inducing genuine change in supply chain partners’ often deeply entrenched operational practices necessitated the implementation of a structured instrument for operationalising the SCoC through consistent assessment and knowledge sharing.
Guided by this understanding, we 
launched a Digital Supply Chain Assessment Project in FY 2024-25.
This Project pursued three strategic aims:
 › T
o assess and quantify the 
sustainability performance of 
major suppliers; › T
o identify material areas for 
improvement and foster the adoption of more responsible practices; and
 › T
o establish a mechanism for 
systematically embedding sustainability considerations into procurement decision-making.
In FY 2025-26, the Project entered its second phase. This year, it assessed and quantified the sustainability performance of 120 major suppliers through self-assessments and synthesised the findings gleaned from these evaluations to formulate tailored, data-driven action plans comprising recommendations they can adopt to strengthen their sustainability practices. In doing so, the Project enhanced visibility into Scope 3 emissions, facilitated the identification of high-risk suppliers with inferior sustainability performance, and provided them with the knowledge and capabilities required to improve ESG awareness and on-the-ground implementation.

MSMEs form a critical part of JSW Steel’s supply chain, and their sustainability performance has a direct bearing on our overall environmental outcomes and ability to meet compliance obligations. Accordingly, we regard strengthening their sustainability capabilities as integral to advancing sustainability objectives across our value chain.
However, MSMEs often lack the technical expertise, institutional capacity, 
and financial resources required to embed sustainability into day-to-day operations. As a result, their ability to implement structured practices across areas such as energy efficiency, water stewardship, emissions reduction, and regulatory compliance frequently remains constrained.
To help address this gap, in FY 2025-26, we conducted an online capacity-
building workshop in collaboration with FICCI, aimed at upskilling MSMEs. The workshop drew on our on-ground sustainability experience and focused on practical, implementable themes, including water conservation and recycling, low-capex energy efficiency measures, renewable energy adoption pathways, carbon footprint reduction strategies, and key environmental compliance frameworks.
The session brought together approximately 70 MSMEs from across our value 
chain. Participants gained actionable insights into integrating sustainability considerations into core business operations, with a particular emphasis on the links between environmental performance, cost efficiency, regulatory preparedness, and operational resilience.
Overall, the workshop served as a targeted capacity-building initiative 
aimed at strengthening foundational sustainability capabilities among our MSME partners, enabling them to better align with evolving environmental expectations and contribute to the development of a more sustainable and resilient supply chain.70 MSMEs upskilled

At JSW Steel Limited, we uphold the 
highest standards of ethics and integrity across all aspects of our operations, guided by a strong culture of transparency and responsible governance. The Board oversees adherence to our Code of Conduct, while employees across our Company remain committed to embedding ethical practices and responsible behaviour in everyday decision-making.
Whistleblower policy
Our Whistleblower Policy offers a secure and confidential platform, operational 24x7, for reporting concerns related to unethical conduct, fraud or violations of the Code of Conduct. During FY 2025-26, the Ethics Helpline received 90 cases, of which 36 remain under review. As of March 31, 2026, 60% of the reported cases had been resolved.
Human rights
We are committed to upholding and advancing human rights across our operations through comprehensive risk assessments and active stakeholder engagement. Detailed evaluations help identify and address potential concerns, supported by a confidential grievance redressal mechanism for the prompt resolution of issues related to discrimination and harassment. Continuous monitoring, audits and awareness programmes strengthen accountability and reinforce a culture of respect and inclusion. We also encourage our suppliers and business partners to follow similar principles, prioritising those aligned with our values. Guided by regulatory requirements and voluntary commitments, we maintain transparent disclosures and uphold a strict stance against discrimination and associations with human rights violations. Our Sustainability Framework further supports continuous improvement and compliance across all operational areas.Sustainability framework
We adhere to the comprehensive Sustainability Framework of the JSW Group, which is implemented consistently across all our locations. This structured framework enables us to effectively manage key sustainability priorities while strengthening our focus on environmental responsibility, social impact and long-term economic resilience, in alignment with our strategic objectives.
Cybersecurity
Cybersecurity remains fundamental to strengthening our digital ecosystem against an increasingly complex threat landscape. Guided by a proactive and forward-looking approach under the oversight of our Chief Information Officer and the Risk Management Committee of the Board, we continue to reinforce the resilience and security of our operations.
Key elements of our approach
Comprehensive risk management
We undertake regular and rigorous assessments to identify potential vulnerabilities and address emerging risks, ensuring the protection of critical assets, systems and information across our operations.
Adherence to industry standards
Our cybersecurity framework is aligned with ISO/IEC 27001:2013 and other recognised best practices, enabling strong governance, operational resilience and regulatory compliance.Policy-driven security
Our Cyber Security Policy, readily accessible through internal digital platforms, clearly outlines responsibilities, protocols and controls, promoting transparency, accountability and organisation-wide awareness.
Continuous enhancement
Through ongoing system upgrades, regular monitoring and proactive interventions, we continuously strengthen our cybersecurity infrastructure to stay prepared for evolving digital threats.Contributions to institutions, bodies and political parties

Comprehensive tax-related disclosures are provided in Form AOC, forming an integral part of our Annual Report. Further strengthening our commitment to transparency and accountability, our Tax Transparency Report outlines our tax principles, governance framework and related policies, while also providing quantitative insights into our financial contributions across various categories. Through this approach, we continue to promote clarity and build stakeholder confidence in our tax practices and disclosures.
Key memberships
We actively participate in leading trade bodies and industry associations to encourage collaboration, exchange perspectives and contribute to sectoral development. BOARD COMMITTEES
Directors comply with the minimum 
attendance requirements for Board meetings in line with the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 (“the Act”). Pursuant to Section 167(1)(b) of the Act, every Director is required to attend at least one Board meeting held during the year. Over the past three years, the average attendance at Board meetings stood at 94.85%, reflecting the strong engagement and active participation of Board members in our Company’s governance processes. During the reporting year, eight Board meetings were convened, with the minimum attendance by an individual Director being 7.58 out of 8 meetings, representing an attendance rate of 94.75%.Audit Committee (AC)
The Audit Committee, constituted as a sub-committee of the Board of Directors, comprises Independent Directors. The Committee is responsible for overseeing our Company’s financial reporting framework and strengthening the integrity of our governance processes. Its key responsibilities include the review of financial statements, approval of related-party transactions, evaluation of changes in accounting policies and practices, assessment of audit plans and significant audit observations, monitoring the adequacy of internal control systems, ensuring compliance with applicable accounting standards and recommending the appointment of auditors, among other functions.

Independent Assurance Statement   
 
 
 
 
Introduction and Objective of Work 
 
BUREAU VERITAS has been engaged by JSW Steel Limited (hereinafter referred to as “JSW Steel” 
or “the company” ) to provide independent assurance of sustainability disclosures reported in the 
Integrated report of JSW Steel (hereinafter abbreviated as “Report” ) for the reporting period from  
1st April 2025 to 31st March 2026 based on reporting criteria followed for the Integrated report. 
 
Reasonable Assurance is provided for BRSR “Core” and Limited Assurance for BRSR 9 Principles and 
IR prepared in accordance with GRI framework. The verification of the KPI and Sustainability practices 
adopted by JSW Steel at the respective operations and review of documents and non-financial 
disclosures were conducted from December 2025 to June 2026 as a part of reasonable and limited 
assurance of sustainability disclosures. 
 
Intended User 
 
The assurance statement is made solely for “JSW Steel and its stakeholders” as per the governing 
contractual terms and conditions of the assurance engagement contract between “JSW Steel” and “Bureau Veritas”. To the extent that the law permits, we owe no responsibility and do not accept any liability to any party other than “JSW Steel” for the work we have performed for this assurance report, or our conclusions stated in the paragraph below. 
 
Reporting Criteria 
 
The company has adopted the below criteria for preparing the report: 
 
 The International<IR> Framework (January 2021); 
 Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Standards; 
 World Steel Association’s – worldsteel (WSA) Environmental Performance Indicators (GHG 
Emissions); 
 Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol. 
 Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) as per SEBI Latest Master 
Circular No. HO/49/14/14(7)2025-CFD-POD2/I/3762/2026 dated January 30, 2026. 
 
Bureau Veritas conducted reasonable sustainability assurance in accordance with the requirements of International Federation of Accountants (IFAC), International Standard on Assurance Engagement 
(ISAE) 3000 (Revised) Reasonable Assurance & GHG as per ISAE 3410. Under this standard, Bureau 
Veritas has reviewed the information presented in the report against the characteristics of relevance, 
completeness, materiality, reliability, neutrality, and understandability.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
      
 
 
 
Independent Assurance Statement   
 
Scope, Boundary, and Limitations of Assurance 
 
The scope of assurance involves sustainability performance of non-financial disclosures (General and 
Topic Specific as mentioned below) of the following operations in India for the period 1st April 2025 to 
31st March 2026 based on GRI Standards, GHG protocol, and World Steel Association’s (worldsteel) 
Environmental Performance Indicators.  
 JSW Steel Limited’s Integrated Steel Plants at Vijayanagar, Dolvi, Salem. 
 JSW Green Steel Limited earlier known as JSW Salav Works 
 JSW Operational Mines at Vijayanagar & Odisha 
 JSW Steel Coated Products Limited’s (JSW SCPL) operation  
 Amba River Coke Limited’s (ARCL) operations at Dolvi. 
 JSW Industrial Gases Private Limited’s (IGPL), Vijayanagar. 
 JSW Steel Raigarh Works. 
 Bhushan Power & Steel Limited Works (BPSL), Sambalpur 
 
The review of the sustainability performance of non-financial disclosures is limited to the above- 
mentioned operations of JSW Steel only. 
 
The Scope of Sustainability Assurance for IR and BRSR includes: 
 
 An assessment of the procedures or approaches followed for data compilation and reporting of 
the sustainability performance non-financial disclosures for specific operations. 
 Testing, on a sample basis, of evidence supporting the data. 
 Verification of the sample data evidence and information on selected material topics reported 
at the above-mentioned operations for the defined reporting period. 
 Assessment of the suitability between the backup data for the selected sustainability 
performance non-financial disclosures and the information presented in IR. 
 The General and topic-specific sustainability non-financial standard disclosures are subject to 
limited assurance based on the extent of information available for assurance 
 Completion of assurance statement for inclusion in the report reflecting the verification, findings, 
and conclusion of the disclosure’s assurance. Gap assessment as per GRI standards and World Steel Association (worldsteel), highlights of findings during verification of disclosures, draft assurance statement, final signed assurance statement as per GRI standards compliance. 
 The reasonable assurance includes verification of the data and information on following selected material BRSR Core topics: 
 
 Green-house gas (GHG) footprint 
 Water footprint 
 Energy footprint 
 Embracing circularity - details related to waste management by the entity 
 Enhancing Employee Wellbeing and Safety 
 Enabling Gender Diversity in Business 
 Enabling Inclusive Development 
 Fairness in Engaging with Customers and Suppliers 
 Open-ness of business 
 
For IR, the reasonable assurance was conducted for all environmental topics for below listed 
operational locations:

Limitations and Exclusions 
 
The assurance is limited to the above-mentioned scope of work and excludes the information relating 
to: 
 Data related to the Company’s financial performance disclosures. 
 Activities and practices followed outside the defined assurance period stated hereinabove. 
 < 
 Positional statements, expressions of opinion, belief, aim, or future intention by “JSW Steel” and 
statements of future commitment. 
 The assurance does not extend to the activities and operations of “JSW Steel” outside of the 
scope and geographical boundaries mentioned in the report as well as the operations undertaken by any other entity that may be associated with or have a business relationship with “JSW Steel”. 
 Compliance with any Environmental, Social, and legal issues related to the regulatory authority. 
 Any of the statements related to company aspect or reputation. 
 The data reported for 305-3 (Scope-3 GHG emissions) is applicable to Purchased goods and

The methodology adopted for Assurance 
 
Bureau Veritas employs a structured process to assure the accuracy and reliability of sustainability data, 
covering both general and topic-specific disclosures. The specific procedures, their timing, and their extent are tailored to the provided data and evidence. This includes verifying risks associated with 
material non-financial disclosures and their relevance for the reporting period. We also consider JSW 
Steel's internal strategy during report preparation to design and validate appropriate assurance 
procedures.  
Our assurance scope involves examining sample evidence, information, and explanations deemed 
necessary to draw conclusions. These conclusions are based on the following key areas:  
 Reporting Framework Adherence: 
 
o Confirming the report's alignment with Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Standards and 
Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) Standards, including applicable 
BRSR parameters for JSW Steel's operations. 
o Assessing adherence to the BRSR framework for Reasonable Assurance of Core 
parameters, JSW Steel's reporting framework, and the principles of Materiality, Inclusivity, and Responsiveness, along with their stakeholder engagement framework.  
 Data Integrity and Systems:

o Reviewing the report to ensure disclosures are not misrepresented.

o Verifying systems and procedures for quantifying, collating, and analyzing sustainability 
performance disclosures. 
o Assessing the reliability and accuracy of month-wise data. 
 
 
 Strategic Alignment and Stakeholder Engagement:

officials.

stakeholder issues, including performance measurement, target setting, governance, and accountability.

India’s largest steel

material processing, steelmaking and downstream value-added manufacturing, JSW Steel has grown from a single manufacturing unit to become India’s leading integrated steel company with a consolidated crude steel capacity of 33.4 MTPA and 4.5 MTPA through the JSW JFE Steel JV. Joint Venture capacity is also expected to scale up to 16 MTPA by FY 2031-32 driven by planned expansion initiatives. The Company’s plant in Vijayanagar, Karnataka is the largest single-location steel-producing facility in India with a current capacity of 19.5 MTPA.**

JSW JFE Steel Limited (JJSL)

Under this structure, JSW Steel transferred BPSL’s steel business to a dedicated subsidiary to facilitate the joint venture, with JFE committing equity investment for a 50% stake and the partners targeting a meaningful scale-up of the Odisha facility over the medium term, supported by JFE’s advanced process and product technologies.JSW JFE Electrical Steel Nashik

JSW Severfield Structures Limited

REINFORCING COST LEADERSHIP  
THROUGH INTEGRATED MANUFACTURING
JSW Steel has turned into a global leader 
in conversion costs using its operational edge, strategically located facilities, advanced manufacturing capabilities, high workforce productivity and a resilient business model. As an integrated producer, the Company offers a diverse product portfolio, leveraging industry-leading technologies across the value chain. Its operations span from raw material processing such as beneficiation, pelletisation and sintering to downstream value-added products, including cold-rolled, galvanised and colour-coated steel. Strong connectivity through rail, road and port infrastructure ensures reliable supply and lower logistics cost of sourcing raw materials and delivering finished products.
The Company continues to reinforce its 
position among the lowest cost steel producers globally, anchored in its integrated manufacturing model, scale efficiencies and sustained focus on operational excellence. 
Strengthening raw material integration 
remained a key lever for cost stability. Increase in captive iron ore consumption contributing to lower logistics costs and reduced exposure to market volatility. Progress on the 302 km slurry pipeline project in Odisha continued during the year, which management has indicated is expected to deliver logistics cost savings of up to ₹ 1,000 per tonne of iron ore upon 
commissioning, thereby structurally enhancing cost competitiveness. 
Energy optimisation initiatives further 
supported cost efficiencies. The Company commissioned close to 1 GW of renewable energy capacity during the year and has approvals in place for 2.5 GW of renewable generation and 320 MWh of battery storage, enabling a structurally lower energy cost base over the medium term. In parallel, the deployment of AI-enabled digital solutions across operations has improved productivity, asset reliability and maintenance effectiveness, with a potential cost saving as these initiatives scale across locations. 
Collectively, these initiatives enabled 
the Company to partially offset volatility in steel realisations, sustain operating margins and fortify its cost competitiveness and operational resilience during FY 2025-26.
Securing raw material a 
strategic priority  
JSW Steel continued to strengthen raw 
material security during FY 2025-26 through accelerated operationalisation and ramp-up of captive mining assets. Iron ore production from Odisha mines—including Nuagaon, Narayanposhi and Gonua—reached 10.71 MnT during the year, exceeding planned levels, with dispatches of 8.32 MnT to support steelmaking operations.
Regulatory milestones were also 
achieved, including the enhancement of environmental clearance for the Narayanposhi mine from 6 MTPA to 10 MTPA, alongside plans for a large-scale beneficiation facility. These initiatives materially improved captive ore availability and reduced dependence on external procurement.
During the year, the Company also 
advanced geographic diversification of its mining footprint, with the commencement of operations at the Cudnem mine in Goa in November 2025. The mine produced approximately 0.5 MnT of iron ore, with around 0.3 MnT dispatched to the Dolvi

Integration of captive resources with 
steelmaking operations was further strengthened through higher utilisation of internally sourced raw materials, particularly at Vijayanagar, where the Company recorded its highest-ever receipts from captive mines. The Company firmed up its backward integration with 25 iron ore mines and four coking coal mines, enhancing self-sufficiency and reducing reliance on external sources. Out of the 25 iron ore mines, 13 are operational across Karnataka, Odisha and Goa while the rest are at various stages of development and commissioning.
Building long-term raw material 
resilience
JSW Steel has formalised the acquisition 
of the Minas de Revuboè (MdR) Coking Coal Mining Project located in the Moatize coal basin, Tete Province, Mozambique. The MdR mine holds 850 MnT of reserves, with the potential to yield 250 MnT of usable coking coal. The mine will be developed in phases, with the first phase targeted for completion by mid-CY 2028, producing around 5 MTPA of usable coking coal. This marks a significant step in JSW Steel’s Global Raw Material Strategy and India-Mozambique Economic Cooperation. The MdR project is deemed a strategic asset as it provides JSW Steel access to substantial reserves of premium hard coking coal, a key raw material necessary for high-quality steel manufacturing. This long-term supply assurance is expected to provide cost-effective inputs, reducing dependence on other imported coking coal and optimising cost structure over the long term.
Expanding resource depth across 
global and domestic assets
JSW Steel has significantly bolstered its 
position in the Australian metallurgical coal sector by increasing its stake in the Illawarra Coal operations. The transaction involves JSW Steel increasing its stake in the M Res HCC joint venture from 66.7% to 83.3%, to increase its effective economic interest in Illawarra coking coal from approximately 20% to 30%. These mines produce premium hard coking coal.In parallel, statutory clearances were secured for coking coal assets in Jharkhand, supporting planned operationalisation in subsequent periods and strengthening long-term coking coal security. 
Building long-term resource 
resilience
In addition to FY 2025-26 execution, the 
Company continued to build medium-term resource security through capacity augmentation and pipeline development across mining assets. These include beneficiation expansion plans, new mining blocks and infrastructure initiatives to support evacuation and processing. JSW Steel is progressing towards increasing the share of captive raw materials in its overall consumption mix over the medium term, thereby reducing exposure to global price volatility and ensuring sustained support to its long-term capacity expansion strategy.
JSW Steel has set a target of meeting 
about 50% of its iron ore and its coking coal requirements from captive sources, This will be achieved by actively participating in auction of mining assets, by setting up domestic linkages with auctioned coking coal assets, and by acquiring coal washeries to improve quality and supply reliability.THE DIGITAL FOCUS

DECARBONISING 
STEELMAKING
Steelmaking contributes 7-9% of global 
greenhouse gas emissions and acts as a primary industrial source of air pollution, water contamination, and solid waste.
Evolving global regulations are increasingly 
driving the demand for steel with a lower carbon footprint, setting the $77.46 billion global market for green steel on a 55.6% annual growth trajectory to reach $129.08 billion by 2034, according to media reports.
What plays behind this growth is the 
orchestrated effort of most major economies to limit the rise of global temperature below 2 degrees Celsius, if not within 1.5 degrees, as was set by the Paris Agreement.
More than 130 countries have adopted 
net-zero targets, collectively covering approximately three-quarters of global greenhouse gas emissions. While the US, EU and UK have set the deadline for 2050, China has the target for 2060 and India for 2070. Additionally, measures such as the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) are expected to accelerate the growth in global green steel market. In the near term, public sector and infrastructure projects are also likely to progressively mandate the procurement of low-carbon steel.
In alignment with India's commitment 
to achieve net-zero emissions by 2070, JSW Steel has embarked on a US$1 billion decarbonisation programme, targeting a 42% reduction in CO
2 emissions intensity 
by 2030 and net neutral in carbon emissions across all operations under direct control by 2050. The Company is backing its green steel efforts by actively integrating clean energy sources into its operations and exploring innovative solutions across manufacturing and logistics. By optimising its energy mix and increasing the share of renewables, JSW Steel is shrinking its carbon footprint while reaffirming its resilience against energy price volatility and evolving regulatory landscapes. This transition is further backed by cost efficiency, as renewable energy offers a competitive alternative to conventional thermal power.
Keeping up its commitment to helping 
India reach its Net Zero target, JSW Steel has commissioned a pilot project for green hydrogen at Vijayanagar, which is expected to offer a strategic advantage to support future scale-up and low-carbon steelmaking initiatives.07 /  MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS  /  1.0 ORGANISATIONAL OVERVIEW

Global economy 
Over the past few years, the world has 
faced several challenges across multiple fronts. While the Russia-Ukraine conflict continued to simmer, tariff barriers between major economies kept the business environment volatile, creating uncertainty across sectors. 
The global economy, however, showed 
resilience and inched up to 3.4% growth in 2025, keeping up the momentum from the previous year. Policy support in key economies, including rate cuts by central banks amidst easing inflationary headwinds and lower-than-anticipated impact of US tariffs supported growth.
The business environment remained 
volatile as changing tariff rates and shifting announcements caused front-loading of trade in different phases. Another key support to growth came from a spurt in tech sector investments, particularly in the US, which spurred trade of related products. World trade volume (of goods and services) grew 5.1% in 2025, picking up pace from 3.5% in the previous year.
Capital inflow into technology sector 
helped the US economy grow 2.1% in 2025, though the momentum slowed down towards the end of the year because of a 43-day government shutdown. Increased fiscal spending and easy monetary policy helped the Euro area to record an accelerated growth of 1.4%. China recorded a 5% growth sticking to its target for the year, despite sustained weakness in the property market, thanks to resilient exports and government measures to boost consumption. When the US-bound shipments reduced, China diversified exports to other regions, leading to a robust 5.5% growth in its merchandise exports.A growing crisis in the Middle East escalated significantly by February 2026, clouding the world economic outlook, threatening to derail the growth momentum of the previous two years. In this backdrop, the IMF's April 2026 World Economic Outlook, ‘Global Economy in the Shadow of War’, forecast that the global growth would slow down to 3.1% in 2026 from 3.4% a year back. 
The reference scenario assumes that 
the conflict turns out to be short-lived and that average crude oil price for the year settles into low 80s (dollar a barrel). If this assumption does not play out and the conflict or its after-effects drag on longer, then there is a substantial downside risk to the growth projections. The IMF forecasts for 2026 indicate a more pronounced slowdown in Emerging Markets and Developing Economies than in the Advanced Economies.
The conflict has impacted the world 
economy through various channels. The supply shock, particularly impacting the trade flows and production of oil, gas and derivative products, has been severe, causing spikes in energy prices and logistics costs, as well as many secondary quantity and price effects for various commodities down the value chain, including fertilisers, metal products,  
and packaging materials.
These effects are likely to reverse in a 
gradual manner, after the end of military operations, with likely continuation of some geopolitical risk premium into market prices and the lingering effect of physical damages suffered by energy facilities and certain industries in the region during the war.
The supply shock has stalled the process 
of wind-down of inflationary pressures caused by the previous supply chain disruption following the pandemic and then the Ukraine war. The IMF has projected global headline inflation to increase from 4.1% in 2025 to 4.4% in 2026. Inflationary risks during the crisis caused bond yields to harden and monetary policy expectations to turn cautious. While the US Fed was previously expected to continue lowering its policy rate (having cut the policy rate by 75 basis points in 2025), those expectations have been diluted after the war began.
Growth and economic activity is likely 
to suffer due to direct hit to operations in the Middle East (which accounts for 6%+ of the global economy in purchasing power parity terms), slowdown in exports to the region, supply chain disruptions in other parts of the world (particularly, Asia) due to reduced imports from the region, implications of inflation for demand, impact on tourism and related activities and implications of weak financial market sentiment and fragile risk appetite on investments and consumption. Duration of the crisis and the time taken for normalisation of the supply chains are, therefore, a critical determinant of the economic outlook for 2026 and beyond. 
After the US Supreme Court in February 
2026 ruled illegal the so-called ‘reciprocal tariffs’ slapped in 2025, the US government replaced those tariffs with tariffs under other legal provisions and launched trade investigations to restore the earlier rates that differed across countries. This has created a window of about 4-5 months, during which the country’s average effective tariff rate has reduced and tariff level is broadly similar for imports from different countries. While tariffs continue to impact the world economy, their impact has been somewhat diluted in 2026 by this. 
But it has not been all about uncertainties. 
There have been some supportive factors 
for the global economy such as lagged effects of the rate cuts effected earlier in the US and Euro area, momentum of technology sector investments that would lead to productivity gains, and broadly supportive fiscal policies. Fiscal boost from tax incentives in the US, ramping up of infrastructure and defence spending in Europe and fiscal stimulus announced by Japan’s new government are expected to dilute the impact of war. As and when the ongoing military conflicts end, reconstruction of damaged infrastructure could provide impetus to economic activities. 
Beijing has laid out supportive policies 
to back the Chinese government’s 2026 growth target of 4.5-5%. Early data trends during 2026 suggest recovery in the country’s fixed asset investments and strong industrial growth.

Indian economy defied the global 
trends, recorded strong growth of 7.7% in FY 2025-26, surpassing the 7.1% expansion in the previous year, according to the advance estimates of the National Statistical Organisation. Private consumption and capital formation both recorded improved performance. Consumption was helped by supportive policy framework, with personal income tax concessions for the middle class and rationalisation of GST rates, the latter especially helping the economy in the second half of the year.Imposition of steep US tariffs affected merchandise exports, which recorded a minor increase during the year. Services exports, however, recorded a robust growth. Although current account deficit widened to some extent, it remained at a comfortable level. 
Capital expenditure by the central and 
state governments expanded in FY 2025-26, maintaining the momentum of public capex for infrastructure sectors. Fiscal consolidation continued, with the Centre’s fiscal deficit narrowing to an estimated 4.4% of the GDP, with tighter control on non-capex spending. 
Inflation moderated substantially to the 
lower end of the RBI’s tolerance band, averaging just above 2% during the year. GST rate cuts and moderation of food inflation contributed to the low inflation outcome, providing policy space for the RBI to cut its key repo rate by 100 basis points during the year. The rate cuts were front-loaded in the first quarter.
